_anchors.canvas.w: 52. The board is 32 px and the cushion variant swings a leaf 8 px past the right cap at the end of its sway; 52 holds that with the outline ring and margin.
_anchors.canvas.h: 36. A bloom on its stem stands 9 px above the board and the fern's sprig droops 16 px below it. The first value was 32 and the silhouette lock caught two variants painting into row 0 — **a stem lengthened to fix an absent part is a stem that has to fit**, and the two changes belong in the same turn.
_anchors.canvas.originX: canvas.w / 2. A platform is symmetric about the point the game places it at, and the collision rule uses one half-width for all four variants.
_anchors.canvas.originY: 14, and it is ON THE TOP SURFACE of the board. That is the only row of a platform anything cares about, so it is the row the sprite is placed by. Authoring the origin at the centre would make the game responsible for knowing the board's thickness.
_anchors.tones.perMaterial: 5, matching the cat and every other subject since 15/08.
_anchors.frames.walk: 8, matching the cat's cycle so a shelf and the animal on it never beat against each other.
_anchors.gait.swing: 0.09 turns, 32.4 degrees at a key of 1, and it is set by what the SCREEN shows rather than by what a leaf does. A bloom sits 6 to 7 px from the root of its stem, so 32 degrees moves it about 3.5 px over 1.76 s. That is a gentle breeze at this scale. The first pass paired keys of 0.16 with a swing of 0.06 and got three degrees of travel: eight byte-identical frames, and a minimum pair distance of exactly zero from the perception channel. An amplitude below one pixel is not restraint, it is a still image — the astronaut's nine-degree arms, repeated on a plant.
_anchors.gait.lift: 2 px. Unused — no ornament translates — and anchored so a future one has a number to spend.
_anchors.shadow.steps: 6, one more than the cushion's depth radius of 4.2, so the cushion shades the board under it.
_anchors.shadow.strength: 1 ramp step, matching the cat. Same garden, same bounce.
_anchors.fill.weight: 0.16, matching the cat, for the same reason: one scene, one fill.
_anchors.playback.msPerFrame: 220. Eight frames make a 1.76 s sway — slower than the cat's 720 ms tail on purpose, because the plant and the animal are moving for different reasons and matching periods would make them look linked.
_anchors.playback.scale: 4, read only by the bench viewer.
_anchors.light.x: -0.5, and it is byte-identical to `cat.json`. ONE lamp for the whole picture: a shelf lit from a different direction than the animal standing on it is the defect he named on the moon, one scene earlier.
_anchors.light.y: -0.72, identical to `cat.json`. Late afternoon in a garden: the light comes down through leaves rather than in from a low sun.
_anchors.light.z: -0.3, identical to `cat.json`. A little front light so the near face of a round mass keeps reading.
_anchors.light.curve: 1.1, identical to `cat.json`. Near linear, because the wood's own range is wide enough not to need the ramp bent.
_anchors.body.scale: 1. The board is 32 px against a 200 px world, so six of them would span it. Two shelves side by side must not look like a floor, and at a sixth of the width they never do.
_anchors.outline.enabled: true. The 15/08 ink verdict: a drawn line is half of what made the winning sample read. Every subject in this project has carried one since.
_anchors.outline.material: "ink". The palette's own line material, a warm dark brown rather than a black — a neutral line against a warm coat would be the one cool thing in the picture.
_anchors.outline.inner: true. Moss on a plank, a cushion on a plank and a leaf on a stem are all one object overlapping another, and the inner line is what says there are two of them.
_anchors.outline.rim: false. `rim` and `enabled` are the two answers to the same question and this project settled on the drawn line on 15/08. Kept expressible so "both" and "neither" stay reachable.
_anchors.shadow.bias: 0.25, the project-wide value since run 7. Depth tolerance, so a curved surface does not shadow itself along its own tangent.
_anchors.fill.x: 0.45, opposite the key in x. A fill is what a photographer puts across from the key light and what a painter calls bounce.
_anchors.fill.y: 0.5, from BELOW. The key comes down through leaves and the bounce comes up off the ground, which is what an outdoor scene actually does.
_anchors.fill.z: -0.3, matching the key's own z. The fill is a weaker second lamp, not a different camera.
